doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Young musicians then and now
summary: Mead compares music-making among young people today with his youth and his sons' era.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you think there’s a difference now with — music is so available in huge quantities to younger people through iPods and internet and the whole thing, where during your era and my era it was not so getable all the time. Do you think it makes a difference?

Well I’m not sure. That’s an interesting hypothesis. Something that I’ve noticed through the years is when I was growing up playing a musical instrument was kind of a big deal and many people did that. And of course it was the era of a town bands and all of that. I notice today in Vermont that’s very true. There are lots and lots of young musicians, middle school kids, who really are great players and who take great pride in their playing. Interestingly when my boys were at that stage, and so that was more in the seventies, sports seemed to be more important. And so I don’t know if that’s a biased thing I’m

seeing where I live or if there’s something to that. But I would say that I don’t think there’s a big difference between today and the old days. I think there are a lot of really good musicians around and I think ultimately live music is what’s exciting and what makes it work. So I’m looking for a resurgence if you will, when all these young cats get out of school and get to play, and maybe we’ll see more of that. But I certainly agree with you. It seemed like in the seventies and eighties it was more we listened to music rather than played it. It would be fun to get back to the playing it.
